content_voiceover: This diagram walks through the platelet adhesion cascade at a site of vessel injury, moving left to right with blood flow. First, circulating platelets tether loosely to von Willebrand factor exposed on the subendothelium through the platelet receptor GP1b. That interaction is low affinity and shear dependent, so platelets don't stick firmly, they roll along the surface, slowing down. As they roll over exposed collagen, receptors like GPVI and integrin alpha2 beta1 engage collagen directly, converting rolling into firm adhesion. Once adherent, platelets activate, change shape, and recruit more platelets through GPIIb-IIIa binding fibrinogen, building the aggregate into stable adhesion. Board relevance, this VWF-GP1b axis is the basis of von Willebrand disease and Bernard-Soulier syndrome, while the GPIIb-IIIa aggregation step is deficient in Glanzmann thrombasthenia and is the target of drugs like abciximab and tirofiban.
keypoint_voiceover: Remember the two receptor pairs. GP1b binding VWF gives rolling and adhesion, and its deficiency causes Bernard-Soulier syndrome. GPIIb-IIIa binding fibrinogen gives aggregation, and its deficiency causes Glanzmann thrombasthenia. That contrast is a classic board pairing, one affects adhesion, the other affects aggregation, and GPIIb-IIIa is also the pharmacologic target of the antiplatelet agents abciximab, eptifibatide, and tirofiban.
